prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials in this search yet, and the starting network scored 0.000 on both seeds. Across earlier searches, only one network family ever scored above 0. It feeds the legal-action mask in as input channels under several spatial layouts, and its per-layout output maps are mapped back to the action layout and summed. In one world it reached 0.22 dev success. Recipe-only changes, other heads and other trunks all gave exactly 0. This suggests the world's action layout does not match how the observation is described. The mask is the only input that is guaranteed to be laid out like the actions, so the network can use it to learn how the two layouts line up. This round has three tests. The first rebuilds that family to check whether it covers this world. The second widens the hedge to all 8 dihedral layouts in case this world uses a rotation. The third keeps the first network and only lowers the PPO epochs from 4 to 2, which gives about 1.85 times as many samples. The first nonzero training success is the signal to watch.

### Round 2
Both mask-layout rebuilds are effectively 0. The 4-layout replica scored 0 under both 4 and 2 PPO epochs. The 8-layout version scored 0.002, which is 2 of 512 designs on one seed and indistinguishable from noise. So this world's deviation is probably not a dihedral relabelling of the action grid, or at least not only that. One plausible deviation the dihedral family cannot express is a different order of the flat action index. For example, the type could be the fastest-varying index (a = (y*X + x)*T + t) rather than the slowest. Reshaping the mask as [T, Y, X] would then scramble it, and so would mapping the outputs back the same way. The fix is cheap: feed the mask, and map the outputs back, under several index orders combined with flips, and sum the logits. I also give the 8-layout network more samples (2 epochs) in case its faint signal is real but slow to learn. As before, I treat nonzero training success as the first real signal.

### Round 3
Every trial has scored about 0 in both training and dev. The one exception is a single seed of r1c2 that built 2 of 512 designs, which is probably luck. r2c2 runs the same 8-layout network with 2 PPO epochs and scored 0. r2c3 covered all 6 orderings of the action index with 4 flips each, which includes every rotation and reflection of the grid, and it also scored 0. So this world probably does not just relabel the type, y and x axes of the action index. Changing the recipe alone will not help while the network cannot line actions up with cells. Two deviations remain untested. (1) DONE may sit at index 0, which shifts every placement index by one; a 3x3 conv cannot follow that shift where rows wrap around. (2) The observation grid may be shifted, rolled or permuted against the action grid by more than the trunk's 5x5 receptive field. I test each one separately, plus a broad combined hedge.

### Round 4
After 9 trials, only r1c2 and r3c1 scored, each with one seed at about 0.004 (about 2 of 512 dev designs). Only r3c1 showed any training success (0.0012). That is noise-level, the same as the starting net's 0. Covering more layouts did not help: 16 and 24 index orders, a DONE-first set, a 48-layout set, and axial row/column mixing for rolls all scored 0. More samples did not help either: 2-epoch runs of 4- and 8-layout nets also scored 0. So a relabelling of the action index probably does not explain this world's zeros, or the task here is simply harder than in the world where the family scored 0.22. Learning itself looks like the bottleneck. With this last round I test three things on the 8-layout dihedral base, which keeps the layout hedge: a deeper trunk that sees the whole grid, a longer credit horizon for the exact-build bonus, and per-layer reasoning about where a brick lands and what it seals. Any 2-seed result above 0.002 beats the current best.

## Trial it ended with
name: mask 8-layout dihedral
hypothesis: Same network, but the mask input and the output maps use all 8 combinations of transpose, y-flip and x-flip (4 flips if the grid is not square). This covers rotations and double flips that the 4-layout version cannot express, at almost the same compute. If it beats the replica, this world uses a layout outside the 4. It is refuted if it scores 0 while the replica scores above 0, or if both score 0.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 3 guesses the right kind of change: "The observation grid may be shifted, rolled or permuted against the action grid by more than the trunk's 5x5 receptive field." Round 4 says "axial row/column mixing for rolls" scored 0. Neither round gives the specifics: a wraparound shift of 4 columns to the right, (x+4) mod 8, in the same row. The text also never commits to this idea, and the final trial tests dihedral layouts instead.
